messages.content: Recessions have multiple causes: Demand shocks (sudden fall in spending — household confidence collapses, investment freezes). Supply shocks (sudden increase in input costs — 1973 oil embargo). Financial crises (credit contraction as banks fail or restrict lending — 2008). Policy mistakes (excessive tightening — US Federal Reserve contributed to 1930s Great Depression). External shocks (pandemic-induced economic halt — 2020). Debt cycles (Dalio's model — credit expansion creates growth, debt service eventually exceeds income, contraction follows). Most recessions involve multiple interacting causes rather than a single trigger.
What is moral hazard and give an example?

Moral hazard: when a party takes more risks because they don't bear the full costs of those risks — usually because someone else does. Examples: banks with implicit government guarantees take excessive risks (privatise gains, socialise losses — 2008 crisis). Insured individuals take less care with insured assets. An employee on a fixed salary has less incentive to maximise effort than a profit-sharing partner. Solutions: align incentives (skin in the game), deductibles and co-pays, performance-based compensation, and regulatory constraints on risk-taking.
What is game theory and what is the prisoner's dilemma?

Game theory studies strategic interactions where each player's outcome depends on others' choices. Prisoner's dilemma: two suspects interrogated separately. If both stay silent: both get 1 year. If both confess: both get 5 years. If one confesses while other stays silent: confessor goes free, silent one gets 10 years. Rational strategy for each individual: confess (dominant strategy). Collective outcome: both confess, both get 5 years — worse than if both cooperated. Dilemma: individual rationality produces collective irrationality. Applications: arms races, price competition, climate agreements, corporate advertising spending.
Explain the concept of opportunity cost.

Opportunity cost: the value of the best alternative foregone when making a choice. It is always present even when no money changes hands. Choosing to attend university: tuition + living costs (explicit costs) + salary you could have earned (opportunity cost). A business using its own building doesn't pay rent, but the opportunity cost is the rental income forgone. Economic profit = accounting profit − opportunity costs. A business earning £50K profit when its capital could earn £80K invested elsewhere is economically loss-making. Sound decision-making requires including opportunity cost, not just explicit cost.
